newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Senior U.N. official frustrated at Earth Summit.
newsitem.headline: Senior U.N. official frustrated at Earth Summit.

text.p: With the Earth Summit only a few days away, the president of the U.N. General Assembly expressed frustration that rich states had not agreed on targets to improve the world's environment and help economies of developing nations.
"So let us not expect anything big," said Razali Ismail, a prime mover in organising the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago and chairman of next week's session.
"There has been a lot of inward-looking, a lot of parochialism among the industrialised countries, who have been taking care of themselves," he told a news conference.
"At the moment, this is all very murkey. We need to have targets and priorities for this session," he said.

More than 65 world leaders, including President Clinton, will gather at the United Nations from June 23-27 to evaluate the decisions taken at the landmark conference in Rio, aimed at preserving the environment for future generations.

To date the conference has been nearly stalemated because of anger among developing nations that aid targeted to improving the environment has not been forthcoming from rich countries, responsible for most of the world's pollution.

In fact, the level of non-military assistance has dropped among northern industrial nations, particularly in the United States, Razali said. Poor states argue that if the North achieved economic growth by polluting the globe, they need some assistance in order not to travel the same route.

"There was a clear understanding in Rio that the model of development in the North was no longer tenable because it depleted a lot of resources," Razali told a press conference. "But there has been a lot of backpedaling."

As an indication of the frustration among developing states, Razali said many were not sending the same top level delegations they had dispatched to Rio, including his own government of Malaysia as well as India.
He said Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad told him that there had been too much "fudging" on many of the promises made in Rio and that "countries of the South have been given a bad deal."

He said he hoped the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations meeting in Denver would come up with language that would inspire confidence, although he suspected "there will be no decisions like that."

But he said he hoped that one or two leaders would come out and say, "I will commit my country to reverse the decline in official development assistance and I will do it even if the others do not come along with me."
He pointed to Japan and Germany, who want permanent seats on the 15-member Security Council, saying that "there is no reason why they cannot commit themselves more than the rest of their colleagues."
Razali also said it was time for the North to further reduce so-called greenhouse gas emissions, like carbon dioxide, believed responsible for climate changes.
The European Union has proposed targets but Japan, Canada and United States, which alone is responsible for 23 percent of the world's carbon emmissions, have not agreed.

Razali said there would be progress in the summit on guidelines for increasing fresh water supplies as well movement on radioactive waste. Protecting the world's dwindling forests and other issues were not yet decided.

But he said the conference failed to include meaningful language on high military expenditures around the world drawing funds away from environmentally-safe development. "I think it is a kind of political amnesia not to disucss this. I think that this is not honest," he said.
